codeFreq.howIntro: Each cell shows how much of a document a code covers, as a percentage. Where a code’s codings overlap, the overlap counts once. What 100% is depends on the kind of document:
codeFreq.howSurvey: Survey: all of the characters of its open-ended answers.
codeFreq.howMedia: Audio and video: the length of the recording. A coding made on the timeline counts for its own time; one made on the transcript, for the time of the lines it covers. If a coding can’t be placed in time, because the transcript has no timestamps, the transcript’s characters are measured instead.
codeFreq.howPdfText: PDF, text codings: all of the characters of the PDF’s text.
codeFreq.howPdfRegion: PDF, box codings: the area of all of its pages.
codeFreq.howPdfMixed: PDF, both: where a code has both text and box codings in a PDF, the average of the two percentages.
codeFreq.howImage: Image: its area, so a box covering half of the image is 50%.
codeFreq.howGroups: Columns marked “(average)” hold several documents and show the average of their percentages, so each document counts equally, however long it is.
codeFreq.howEstimated: If an image’s or page’s size, or a recording’s length, can’t be read from its file, it is estimated from what was coded, and noted below the table.
codeFreq.estimatedNote: The size of {{names}} couldn’t be read (an image’s or page’s area, or a recording’s length), so it was estimated from what was coded.
codeFreq.averageTitle: the average of its documents’ percentages, each document counting equally

intercoder.dropHint: Click Add projects to add each coder's .qdpx file.
intercoder.dropDocuments: Drag documents or folders here from the Document Browser.
intercoder.dropCodes: Drag codes here from the Code Browser.
intercoder.docInProjects_one: In {{count}} of {{total}} projects. Click to see which.
intercoder.docInProjects_other: In {{count}} of {{total}} projects. Click to see which.
intercoder.textDiffersTitle: This document's text isn't the same in every project, so its text codings can't be compared.
intercoder.howCalculated: What do these results mean, and how are they calculated?
intercoder.choiceCharacters: Characters goes through the documents piece by piece (every character of text, every moment of a recording, every point of a page or image) and asks whether both coders coded it the same way. Where a passage starts and stops matters.
intercoder.choiceSegments: Segments takes the coded passages one at a time and asks whether the other coder coded the same passage with the same code. Small differences at a passage’s edges don’t matter, within the Overlap you choose.
intercoder.choiceBoth: Characters gives kappa and alpha, the figures most often reported; Segments helps you find the passages worth discussing. Many teams use both.
intercoder.diagramCharacters: Each character is compared on its own: green where the coders agree (pale where neither coded it), red where only one coded it.
intercoder.diagramSegments: Each passage is compared whole. These two share {{shared}} of the {{union}} characters either coded ({{pct}}), so they match only if Overlap is {{pct}} or less.
intercoder.meaningAgreement: Agreement is how much of the documents the two coders treated the same way: both applied the code, or both left it out. It reads high, because most of a document usually has no code, and leaving it out counts as agreeing.
intercoder.meaningKappa: Kappa is how much better the coders agreed than chance would give, if each had coded as much as they did but in random places. 1 is complete agreement, 0 no better than chance, and below 0 worse. It is the fairer figure to report.
intercoder.meaningExample: For example, take an interview of 100 lines. If one coder codes 5 lines and the other codes 5 different lines, they still agree on the 90 lines neither coded, so agreement is 90%. But they never agreed on what to code, so kappa is about −0.05.
intercoder.meaningScale: As a rough guide, a kappa of 0.80 or more shows strong agreement, 0.60 to 0.79 moderate agreement, and below 0.60 weak agreement: a sign that the code is worth discussing. The table’s colours follow these bands.
intercoder.meaningAlpha: Alpha, shown for three or more coders, reads like kappa, but for all of the coders at once.
intercoder.meaningSegments: Agreement is the share of all the segments both coders coded that the other coder matched, with the same code on nearly the same passage. The kappa below the table reads like the kappa for Characters, but counts segments.
intercoder.meaningOverlap: Overlap sets how nearly the same two passages must be to match. Say one coder codes words 1 to 10 and the other words 2 to 10: they share 9 of the 10 words, so they match at an Overlap of 90% or less. Had the other coded words 1 to 20, they would share 10 of 20 words and match only at 50% or less. At 100%, only exactly the same passage matches.
intercoder.meaningSegmentScale: As a rough guide, segment agreement of 80% or more is good, 70% to 79% workable, and below 70% worth discussing. The table’s colours follow these bands. It depends on Overlap: at 90%, coders must mark almost the same stretch. If agreement rises a lot at a lower overlap, the coders mostly differ about where passages begin and end, not about what they mean.
intercoder.meaningAvgAgreement: With three or more coders, Average agreement shows how well pairs of coders agree on average: the mean of every pair’s agreement, each pair counting equally.
intercoder.infoUnits: Every unit of a document — a character of text, a millisecond of audio or video, a point² of a PDF page, a pixel of an image — is coded or not by each coder. For a pair of coders that gives a 2×2 table: a both coded it, b only the first, c only the second, d neither; n = a + b + c + d.
intercoder.infoKappa: Cohen’s kappa = (po − pe) ÷ (1 − pe), where po = (a + d) ÷ n and pe = [(a + b)(a + c) + (c + d)(b + d)] ÷ n². Shown as – when nobody applied the code, as chance agreement is then total.
intercoder.infoAlpha: Krippendorff’s alpha (three or more coders) = 1 − (n − 1)·o₀₁ ÷ (n₀·n₁), counting every coder’s coding of every unit: o₀₁ the coded/uncoded coincidences, n₁ and n₀ the coded and uncoded values.
intercoder.infoTotals: A code’s row pools every document’s units, so a long document counts for more than a short one. A code applied in more than one kind of unit (text, time, area) averages their proportions. Each code is compared only in the kinds of unit it was applied in.
intercoder.infoAllCodes: All codes: pooled kappa (de Vries et al., 2008) = (mean po − mean pe) ÷ (1 − mean pe), the means taken over the codes; % agreement is the mean po. Alpha likewise: 1 − mean observed ÷ mean expected disagreement.
intercoder.infoSegments: Each coded segment is agreed when the other coder applied the same code to a segment that overlaps it by at least the threshold — the overlap ÷ the span the two cover together. % agreement = agreed segments ÷ all segments, both coders’ counted.
intercoder.infoAvgAgreement: Average agreement (three or more coders) = the mean of the pairs’ % agreement.
intercoder.infoBp: Brennan & Prediger’s kappa (below the table) = (po − 1/k) ÷ (1 − 1/k): po the % agreement over all codes, k the number of codes compared, so chance is picking one of k codes at random. Segments only one coder coded count as disagreements here, so it can differ from other programs’ segment kappa; with many codes it is close to % agreement.
intercoder.infoNotes: Documents in at least two of the projects. Where a document’s text differs between projects, only its time ranges and areas are compared. Where a recording was coded both on its transcript and on its timeline, its transcript codings are compared by the times of their lines. Codings past the end of a document stop at its end. A page’s area or a recording’s length that couldn’t be read is estimated from what was coded, and noted below the results.
intercoder.docNotShared: In only one project, so it can’t be compared.
intercoder.pickDocuments: Drag the documents to compare from the Document Browser into Documents.
intercoder.pickCodes: Drag the codes to compare from the Code Browser into Codes.
intercoder.measureCharactersTitle: Compare every character, second or pixel: % agreement and Cohen's kappa for each pair of coders, and Krippendorff's alpha for three or more
intercoder.measureSegmentsTitle: Compare coded segments: a segment agrees when the other coder's segment of the same code overlaps it enough
intercoder.thresholdTitle: How much two segments must overlap to agree: the shared part as a share of both together
intercoder.codeTitle: The codes you compared. Click the arrow beside a code to see its results in each document
intercoder.allCodersTitle: How well all the coders agree, taken together
intercoder.pairTitle: How well {{first}} and {{second}} agree with each other
intercoder.coderTitle: How well {{name}} agrees with the other coders
intercoder.metricAgreementTitle: How much of the text both coders treated the same way: both coded it, or both left it uncoded. This is always high, because text nobody coded counts as agreement, so it isn’t coloured. Kappa, beside it, is the fairer guide
intercoder.metricSegAgreementTitle: Of all the passages the two coders coded, the share the other coder also coded in nearly the same place (as set by Overlap). Green from 80%, amber from 70%, red below
intercoder.metricKappaTitle: How well the two coders agree, after allowing for the agreement you’d expect by luck alone. 1 means they agree completely, 0 no better than luck. Green from 0.80, amber from 0.60, red below
intercoder.metricAlphaTitle: How well all the coders agree together, after allowing for the agreement you’d expect by luck alone. 1 means complete agreement, 0 no better than luck. Green from 0.80, amber from 0.60, red below
intercoder.metricAgreedTitle: How many of the two coders’ passages the other coder also coded in nearly the same place
intercoder.metricSegmentsTitle: How many passages the two coders coded between them
intercoder.metricAvgAgreementTitle: How well the coders agree on average: the average of every pair’s agreement. Green from 80%, amber from 70%, red below
intercoder.viewCodersTitle: Compare each coder with all the others
intercoder.metricCoderSegAgreementTitle: How well this coder agrees with the others on average: the average of their agreement with each other coder. Green from 80%, amber from 70%, red below
intercoder.metricCoderKappaTitle: How well this coder agrees with the others on average, after allowing for the agreement you’d expect by luck alone. 1 means complete agreement, 0 no better than luck. Green from 0.80, amber from 0.60, red below
intercoder.metricAlphaWithoutTitle: How well the other coders agree among themselves when this coder is left out. Its colour describes the others, not this coder. The number in brackets shows whether this coder is out of step
intercoder.metricAlphaChangeTitle: How much agreement changes when this coder is left out. + means the others agree better without them. Red (+0.10 or more) or amber (+0.05 or more) suggests this coder codes differently from the rest
intercoder.meaningByCoder: With three or more coders, By coder compares each coder with all the others. For Characters it shows the coder’s Average kappa with each of the others, and Alpha without: the alpha of everyone else with this coder left out. For Segments it shows the coder’s Average agreement with each of the others. A coder whose averages are low, or without whom alpha rises, codes least like the rest of the team.
intercoder.meaningAlphaWithoutColours: The shading of Alpha without shows how well the other coders agree among themselves, on the same scale as alpha. Whether this coder is out of step shows in the change in brackets: red when agreement is 0.10 or more higher without them, amber when 0.05 or more. Smaller changes are usually chance.
intercoder.infoByCoder: Average agreement and Average kappa = the mean of the values of every pair the coder is in, each pair counting equally. Alpha without = Krippendorff’s alpha, as above, over the other coders only.

intercoder.resultsPoppedOut: The results are open in a separate window.

intercoder.noDisagreements: The two coders agree everywhere here.
